subject: Science
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 45 minutes × 13 periods = 585 minutes
Total: 13 periods · 9h 45min

periods.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of electric current
periods.activity_title: Compass Under Wire: Catching Current in the Act
periods.activity_description: Students assemble a simple circuit with a battery, switch, and connecting wire, then place a magnetic compass beneath the wire. They observe the needle deflecting when the switch is closed and returning when it is opened, recording what they see before drawing an initial conclusion.

roles.role_description: Sets up the circuit as a shared class reference and prompts students to predict what will happen before closing the switch.
Assemble their own circuits, place the compass, close and open the switch multiple times, and record deflection observations in a table.

time_bands.activity: Teacher demonstrates the exhibition electromagnet story from the chapter opening, then poses the central question: does electric current produce a magnetic effect?
Groups assemble the circuit and compass setup, make a prediction, then close and open the switch while observing and recording the needle's response.
Groups compare their recorded observations and identify the pattern: needle deflects with current, returns without it.
Class discussion consolidates the key concept — a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that disappears when current stops — and introduces the term magnetic field.

periods.teacher_notes: This opening unit anchors the entire chapter by giving students a direct, repeatable observation of the magnetic effect before any explanation is offered. A common error to watch for: students may think the wire itself is a magnet even without current — encourage them to test the wire with the switch open first, so they see the effect is current-dependent, not a property of the wire alone. Grouping students so that one holds the compass while another operates the switch helps them notice the cause-and-effect timing precisely.
materials: Cardboard strip to hold wire level

periods.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of electric current
periods.activity_title: Nail and Wire: First Encounter with an Electromagnet
periods.activity_description: Students wind insulated wire around an iron nail, connect it to a cell, and test whether the nail picks up iron paper clips when current flows and releases them when current is stopped. They record their findings and generate questions about what variables might affect the strength of attraction.

roles.role_description: Wind wire around the nail, connect the circuit, test with paper clips, and list questions about what might change the effect.
Circulates, prompts groups to articulate their observations as cause-and-effect statements, and collects student-generated questions on the board.

time_bands.activity: Brief recap of the previous unit's compass deflection observation; teacher poses the question of whether a wire-wrapped nail could become a temporary magnet.
Groups wind wire around iron nails, connect to a single cell, bring the nail near paper clips, and observe what happens when the switch is closed and opened.
Groups record observations in a two-column table (switch closed / switch open) and generate a short list of 'what if' questions — what if we use more turns? more cells?
Class shares questions; teacher lists them visibly, explaining that the next unit will investigate some of these through a structured activity.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit builds directly on the previous unit's compass deflection: students now see the magnetic effect strong enough to lift objects, which raises the question of what controls its strength. Watch for students who wind the wire in alternating directions — this cancels the magnetic effect and they will see no attraction; redirect them to wind consistently in one direction. Collecting student-generated questions at the close positions the next unit as an investigation the students themselves have called for.

periods.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of electromagnets
periods.activity_title: Coil on a Cylinder: Building a Stronger Electromagnet
periods.activity_description: Students wind a coil on a paper cylinder, place compasses at both ends, and observe field direction. They then insert an iron nail into the core and compare the compass deflection with and without the core, recording data to classify whether the coil with core behaves like a bar magnet.

roles.role_description: Construct the cylindrical coil, position compasses at both ends, insert the iron core, and record deflection angles before and after insertion.
Demonstrates how to read compass orientation at each end and introduces the idea that a coil with two distinct ends might behave like a bar magnet.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recaps the nail electromagnet from the previous unit and introduces the cylindrical coil design, showing how winding wire on a paper tube creates a more uniform field.
Groups wind the coil, connect it to the circuit, place compasses at each end, and record observations; they then slide the iron nail in and record whether deflection increases.
Groups complete a comparison table: coil without core versus coil with core, noting deflection strength and the direction each compass points.
Class shares data; teacher introduces the formal definition of an electromagnet and explains why an iron core increases magnetic strength.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit introduced the electromagnet informally; this unit formalises it by having students produce data that directly supports the definition. The most common misconception here is that any metal core will increase strength — students may suggest using a copper or aluminium core; encourage them to reason from the chapter's explanation that only iron (a ferromagnetic material) behaves this way. Checking that the compass needles at each end point in opposite directions is a good checkpoint that the coil is correctly wound and behaving like a bar magnet.

periods.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of electromagnets
periods.activity_title: Finding the Poles: North, South, and Current Direction
periods.activity_description: Students use a compass to identify which end of their electromagnet is the North pole and which is the South pole, then reverse the current direction by swapping battery terminals and re-identify the poles, recording whether reversal consistently switches the poles.

roles.role_description: Test each end of their electromagnet with a compass, label the poles, swap battery connections, and re-test to determine whether the poles have reversed.
Prompts groups to predict before swapping whether the poles will reverse, stay the same, or behave unpredictably, then facilitates a class comparison of predictions with results.

time_bands.activity: Recap of the previous unit's result that the coil-with-core has two distinct ends; teacher asks: if it is like a bar magnet, does it have a North and South pole?
Groups use the compass to identify and label each pole of their electromagnet, recording their method and result.
Groups predict what will happen when they swap the battery terminals, then perform the reversal and re-identify the poles, recording whether their prediction was confirmed.
Class shares results; teacher consolidates the rule — reversing current reverses the poles — and connects it to the broader property that electromagnet behaviour depends on current direction.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit deepens the classification work of the previous unit by giving students evidence that electromagnet poles are not fixed but current-dependent — a key distinguishing property from permanent magnets. Watch for groups who swap only one wire rather than reversing the battery orientation; ensure they understand that reversing current means changing which terminal the current enters from. A probing question at the close — 'could you make this electromagnet point North on command?' — bridges naturally toward the next unit's investigation of strength variables.
materials: Extra connecting wires to allow terminal swap

periods.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of electromagnets
periods.activity_title: Stronger or Weaker? Investigating Cells and Turns
periods.activity_description: Students systematically vary the number of cells in the circuit and then the number of coil turns, measuring strength by counting how many paper clips the electromagnet holds in each condition, and organising results into a data table to identify the pattern.

roles.role_description: Run a controlled investigation varying one factor at a time — first cells, then turns — and record clip counts in a structured data table.
Introduces the importance of changing one variable at a time and guides groups to keep the unvaried factor constant while they change the other.

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the student-generated questions from the second unit and frames today's investigation: can we test the effect of cells and turns in a systematic way?
Groups test with one cell then two cells, keeping the number of turns constant, and record paper-clip counts for each condition.
Groups now keep cells constant and vary the number of turns (e.g., 10, 20, 30 turns), recording clip counts at each level.
Groups write a two-sentence conclusion for each variable and share with the class; teacher consolidates: more current and more turns both increase electromagnet strength.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit directly addresses the student-generated questions raised in the second unit, giving the investigation a sense of purposeful closure. The most common error is varying both cells and turns simultaneously, producing uninterpretable data — circulate early to check that each group is holding one variable constant. Requiring a written conclusion sentence per variable before sharing forces students to articulate the pattern rather than just read off numbers.

periods.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of electromagnets
periods.activity_title: Lifting Electromagnets and Earth's Giant Magnet
periods.activity_description: Students examine how industrial lifting electromagnets apply the properties investigated so far — controlled by switching current on and off to grip and release heavy metal loads — and then encounter the Earth's magnetic field as arising from the same principle: moving currents of liquid iron in Earth's core generating a magnetic field.

roles.role_description: Leads a structured explanation of industrial lifting electromagnets and the Earth-as-magnet concept, connecting both to the electromagnet properties students have already established.
Complete a guided note frame connecting each industrial/natural application to at least one property of electromagnets they investigated.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the crane-mounted lifting electromagnet: the operator switches current on to grip and off to release, and connects this to the current-dependent field property established in earlier units.

Teacher presents the Earth-as-magnet sidebar: liquid iron currents in Earth's core generate a magnetic field, making Earth behave like a giant electromagnet — students connect this to the coil-with-current model.
Students individually complete a guided note frame: for each application (crane, Earth), they identify which electromagnet property makes it work and whether a permanent magnet could substitute.
Pairs compare their note frames and discuss whether a permanent magnet could replace the crane's electromagnet, sharing one reason with the class.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous four units were entirely hands-on; this unit consolidates that learning by connecting it to real applications, so the didactic approach is appropriate here. Students often think Earth's magnetic field comes from a solid permanent magnet inside the Earth — the chapter explicitly explains it arises from moving liquid iron, which is the same current-produces-field principle they have just investigated. The pair discussion question about whether a permanent magnet could substitute for the crane electromagnet is a diagnostic check: students who understand current-dependence will recognise that a permanent magnet cannot be switched off on demand.
materials: Guided note frame (printed or drawn on board)

periods.stage_label: Observe, record, and explain the heating effect of electric current
periods.activity_title: Nichrome Gets Warm: Observing the Heating Effect
periods.activity_description: Students connect a nichrome wire in a circuit, carefully touch it before and after closing the switch, and record their observation that the wire warms when current flows. They then compare heating when one cell is used versus two, recording qualitative results.

roles.role_description: Assemble the nichrome-wire circuit, perform the before-and-after touch test, and record observations for one-cell and two-cell conditions.
Demonstrates safe touch technique — brief, gentle contact on the side of the wire — and ensures groups record both conditions before discussing.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the new section by asking what happens to a wire when current flows — pivoting from the magnetic effect to a different observable consequence, framing it as a second effect to investigate.
Groups connect the nichrome wire, touch it before closing the switch (no warmth), close the switch and carefully touch again (warmth detected), and record both observations.
Groups repeat the test with two cells, recording whether the wire feels warmer, cooler, or the same compared to the one-cell trial.
Class shares results; teacher introduces the term heating effect of electric current and explains the resistance mechanism: the conductor resists current flow, converting electrical energy to heat.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the second major strand of the chapter, so the teacher_notes should orient students to the shift from magnetic to heating effects while connecting the underlying cause — electric current through a conductor — as the common thread. The key misconception to address is that all wires heat equally; the chapter explains that the heating depends on material, thickness, length, and current, so emphasise that nichrome is chosen for its high resistance, not that all wires behave the same. Ensure students record the before-switch-close observation explicitly — without it, they cannot make the before/after comparison that establishes the causal link.

periods.stage_label: Observe, record, and explain the heating effect of electric current
periods.activity_title: Why Does Wire Heat Up? Connecting Resistance to Heat
periods.activity_description: Students examine what properties of a conductor determine how much heat it produces, working from the chapter's factors — material, thickness, length, current magnitude, and duration — to classify which increase heating and which decrease it, then explain the resistance mechanism in their own words.

roles.role_description: Sort a set of conductor property cards into two groups (increases heating / decreases heating) and write a causal explanation for each grouping.
Provides the property cards and facilitates a whole-class discussion to reconcile disagreements and build a shared explanation of resistance converting electrical energy to heat.

time_bands.activity: Recap of the previous unit: what did we observe, and what term names it? Teacher frames the question for today: what decides how much a conductor heats?

Groups sort property cards — higher resistance material, thinner wire, longer wire, higher current, longer duration, lower resistance material, thicker wire — into 'more heat' and 'less heat' piles, annotating each card with a reason.
Groups write a three-sentence explanation of why a wire heats up, using the words resistance, electrical energy, heat energy, and current.
Class shares explanations; teacher consolidates into the canonical causal statement: resistance converts electrical energy to heat, and more resistance or more current means more heat.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit established the phenomenon; this unit asks students to explain its mechanism — a step up in cognitive demand. The most common confusion is between resistance as a material property and resistance as something that can be changed by circuit design; students may think a longer wire is 'broken' or 'wrong' rather than simply having more resistance. The card-sorting task externalises their reasoning and makes disagreements visible, which is the most productive moment in the unit — encourage groups to articulate why they disagreed rather than just converging on the majority answer.
materials: Property cards (printed or written strips): higher resistance material, thinner wire, longer wire, higher current, longer duration, lower resistance material, thicker wire

periods.stage_label: Observe, record, and explain the heating effect of electric current
periods.activity_title: Useful and Harmful: The Dual Nature of the Heating Effect
periods.activity_description: Students examine how the heating effect is deliberately exploited in household appliances (heaters, stoves, kettles, irons, hair dryers) and also causes problems (energy loss in transmission, overheating, fires), then classify a set of scenarios by whether the heating effect is beneficial or harmful in that context.

roles.role_description: Leads a structured walkthrough of the chapter's appliance examples, explaining what a heating element is and how resistance wire converts electrical energy to heat in each device.
Complete a classification task sorting given scenarios by whether the heating effect is the intended useful output or an unwanted harmful consequence.

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains heating elements in appliances — rod or coil of high-resistance wire — and uses three examples (room heater, electric iron, immersion rod) to show how the heating effect is the intended output.

Teacher presents the problematic side: energy loss in long-distance transmission wires, overheating of small circuit components, and fire risk from overloaded circuits — connecting each to the same resistance-heat mechanism.
Students individually classify eight scenarios (provided on the board) as useful or harmful heating effects, writing a one-sentence justification for each.

Pairs compare classifications; any disagreements are discussed whole-class, with teacher clarifying that the same physical process is useful or harmful depending on whether it is the intended output of the device.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous two units built the mechanistic explanation; this unit applies it to real contexts, which is a higher-demand step. Students often assume the heating effect is always undesirable — a carry-over from experiences of devices overheating — so the teacher should be deliberate about establishing that it is both useful and harmful depending on context. The pair comparison at the close is particularly useful for the scenario of 'wires in a wall getting warm' — some students will classify this as useful (it is warming the room) when it is in fact a harmful energy loss; this disagreement drives productive reasoning.
materials: Board or display with eight application scenarios

periods.stage_label: Explain how cells and batteries supply the current that drives both effects
periods.activity_title: Building a Lemon Cell: Chemistry Makes Current
periods.activity_description: Students construct a Voltaic cell using a lemon, a copper wire, and an iron nail, connect it to an LED, and observe the LED lighting up. They identify the electrolyte (lemon juice), the two electrodes (copper and iron), and record how the cell fits the Voltaic cell model of two different metals in an electrolyte.

roles.role_description: Assemble the lemon cell, connect the LED, observe the result, and label the components on a diagram using the terms electrolyte, positive terminal, and negative terminal.
Introduces the Voltaic cell model before the activity, then connects the lemon cell assembly back to the two-electrode-in-electrolyte structure.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the new section by asking: where does the electric current in a cell come from? Introduces the Voltaic cell model — two different metal electrodes in an electrolyte — and the historical discovery by Volta and Galvani.
Groups push a copper wire and an iron nail into a lemon, connect them to an LED, and observe whether it lights; they adjust connections if needed and confirm the result.

Students draw a labelled diagram of their lemon cell, marking the electrolyte, positive terminal (copper), negative terminal (iron nail), and the direction of current flow through the external circuit.
Class discusses: what would happen over time to the chemicals in the lemon? Teacher introduces the concept that the cell becomes dead when chemicals are consumed.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit opens the third major strand of the chapter — the source of current — and the lemon cell activity makes the abstract idea of chemical-to-electrical energy conversion visible and concrete. A common error is students inserting the copper wire and nail very close together inside the lemon, which can short-circuit the cell and prevent the LED from lighting; guide them to space the electrodes apart. The closing discussion about the cell going dead directly prepares students for the next unit on dry cells and rechargeables.

periods.stage_label: Explain how cells and batteries supply the current that drives both effects
periods.activity_title: Inside a Dry Cell and a Rechargeable Battery
periods.activity_description: Students examine the internal structure of a dry cell — zinc container (negative terminal), central carbon rod (positive terminal), moist paste electrolyte — and compare it with the Voltaic cell and with rechargeable batteries, noting the shift from liquid to paste electrolyte and from single-use to multi-cycle design.

roles.role_description: Guides a structured comparison using a labelled diagram of the dry cell, explaining how the paste electrolyte enables portability and why single-use cells must be replaced while rechargeable ones can be restored.
Complete a three-column comparison table (Voltaic cell / dry cell / rechargeable battery) across four rows: electrolyte type, terminals, reusability, and common applications.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays a labelled cross-section diagram of the dry cell, explaining each component and connecting the structure to the Voltaic cell model built in the previous unit.

Teacher describes rechargeable batteries — from watch-sized to EV-grade — noting that they can be recharged many times but eventually wear out, and introduces Li-ion batteries and solid-state batteries as current and future technologies.
Students individually complete the three-column comparison table, consulting the chapter's content as reference.

Students share one surprising difference they noticed; teacher closes by addressing the safety note: dead batteries are not inert — they contain acids and toxic metals and must go to e-waste recycling.

periods.teacher_notes: The previous unit gave students a working model of the Voltaic cell through direct construction; this unit extends that model to the more common dry cell and rechargeable types, so connecting back to the lemon cell structure is important. Students frequently assume a rechargeable battery is fundamentally different from a dry cell in its chemistry — clarify that the core principle (two electrodes, electrolyte, chemical reaction producing current) is the same; the difference is that the reaction in a rechargeable battery is reversible. The e-waste safety note is brief but important, and ending the unit here ensures it receives attention rather than being rushed.
materials: Labelled dry cell cross-section diagram (board or printed)

periods.stage_label: Reason across both effects to explain how cells and electromagnets work as integrated systems
periods.activity_title: What Happens When? Tracing Current from Cell to Effect
periods.activity_description: Students are given a set of scenario cards describing circuit events — changing cell count, adding turns, switching direction, connecting a nichrome wire — and trace what happens in each case by reasoning from cell to current to the relevant effect (magnetic or heating), justifying each step in writing.

roles.role_description: Work through scenario cards, tracing the causal chain from the cell's current output through to the predicted magnetic or heating effect, writing a justification for each scenario.
Circulates and probes groups with follow-up questions when a justification skips a step in the causal chain, pushing for explicit connections between current magnitude and effect strength.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up the task: all the circuit effects we have studied depend on the same thing — current produced by a cell. Today we trace that chain step by step for a set of new scenarios.

Groups work through four scenario cards, writing a three-step causal chain for each: what does the cell supply? → what changes in the circuit? → what happens to the magnetic or heating effect and why?
Groups share their chains for two scenarios with the class; where chains diverge, teacher facilitates a comparison to identify which step is disputed and why.

Teacher highlights that both the magnetic and heating effects are produced by the same current from the same cell, framing the chapter's integration: the cell is the source, current is the agent, and effects depend on circuit design.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit marks the transition into the final stage — students must now reason across both effects rather than treating them separately. The most common gap is failing to connect cell properties to current magnitude; students may say 'more cells = stronger electromagnet' without articulating that more cells produce higher current which increases the magnetic field. Insisting on explicit three-step chains prevents this shortcut. The closing teacher summary is important: naming the cell as the unifying source across both strands makes the chapter's architecture visible to students before the final unit.

periods.stage_label: Reason across both effects to explain how cells and electromagnets work as integrated systems
periods.activity_title: Design a Circuit: Making Both Effects Work Together
periods.activity_description: Student groups are given a challenge scenario — design a circuit that uses the same cell to operate both an electromagnet (to pick up iron clips) and a heating element (nichrome wire that warms), then predict how changing the cell count will affect both effects simultaneously, justifying predictions with the chapter's causal reasoning.

roles.role_description: Plan and assemble the dual-effect circuit, test it, then make and justify predictions about what increasing the cell count will do to each effect independently.
Facilitates the design discussion by asking groups to commit to a circuit diagram before building, and probes final predictions with 'why does that follow from what you know about current?'

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the challenge: using everything from this chapter, design a single circuit where both the magnetic effect and the heating effect are observable. Groups sketch a circuit diagram first.
Groups assemble their circuit, test that both effects are present (compass deflects at the electromagnet; nichrome wire warms), and adjust connections until both work.
Groups predict in writing what will happen to each effect if cell count is increased, justifying with explicit reference to current, resistance, and magnetic field strength.

Class shares predictions and the reasoning behind them; teacher closes the chapter arc by connecting cells (source), current (agent), and both effects (outcomes) as the integrated story of the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This closing unit requires students to operate both effects in one system, which is the highest-demand task of the chapter — it embodies the dissolution test's requirement to reason across both effects using the cell as the integrating concept. A potential pitfall is that groups wire the electromagnet and nichrome wire in series so that one limits the other; encourage groups to think about whether parallel or series connections serve the challenge better, using their knowledge that current magnitude affects both effects. The prediction-and-justify task at the close is the most important cognitive moment: students who can correctly predict and explain both changes from a single increase in cell count have demonstrated integrated reasoning across the chapter.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of electric current
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students assemble circuits with a compass and then with a wire-wrapped nail to observe directly that current produces a magnetic field that disappears when current stops, and generate questions about what controls the effect's strength.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe, with reference to their own observations, that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field and that the field disappears when the current is switched off.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of electromagnets
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students build a cylindrical-coil electromagnet, identify its North and South poles, reverse the poles by reversing current direction, investigate how cell count and coil turns affect strength, and connect these properties to industrial and natural applications.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify the poles of an electromagnet, demonstrate that reversing the current reverses the poles, and explain how increasing current magnitude or number of turns increases the electromagnet's strength.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Observe, record, and explain the heating effect of electric current
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe nichrome wire heating when current flows, classify the factors that determine how much heat is produced, explain the resistance mechanism, and categorise real-world heating-effect scenarios as useful or harmful.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why a current-carrying conductor heats up in terms of resistance converting electrical energy to heat, and can classify given scenarios as examples of the heating effect being used beneficially or causing harm.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Explain how cells and batteries supply the current that drives both effects
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students construct a lemon Voltaic cell and observe it powering an LED, then compare the Voltaic cell, dry cell, and rechargeable battery on structure, electrolyte type, and reusability through a classification table.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe the structure of a Voltaic cell and a dry cell, explain how a chemical reaction between electrodes and electrolyte produces current, and compare the three cell types on key structural and functional properties.

coverage_handoff.stage_label: Reason across both effects to explain how cells and electromagnets work as integrated systems
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students trace causal chains from cell to current to magnetic or heating effect across scenario cards, then design and build a circuit that demonstrates both effects simultaneously and justify predictions about how changing the cell count affects both effects.
coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can construct and explain an integrated account of how a cell supplies current that produces both magnetic and heating effects, predicting and justifying how changes to cell count, coil turns, or wire material alter each effect.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe, with reference to their own observations, that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field and that the field disappears when the current is switched off.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A magnetic compass is placed directly below a straight wire connected in a circuit with a battery and a switch. The switch is open. When the switch is closed, the compass needle deflects. When the switch is opened again, the needle returns to its original position. What does this sequence of events best demonstrate?

options.label: A
options.text: A current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field that exists only while the current is flowing.

options.label: B
options.text: The battery itself is a magnet and the switch controls how strongly it attracts the compass needle.

options.label: C
options.text: The compass needle deflects because of heat produced by the wire when the switch is closed.

options.label: D
options.text: The wire acts as a permanent magnet that gains strength when the switch is closed.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals a misconception that the wire becomes a permanent magnet — the student has not processed that the effect is current-dependent and reversible.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals confusion between the battery as a source of current and the battery as a source of magnetic effect — the student has not identified the wire (conductor) as the site of the magnetic field.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals a confusion between the magnetic effect and the heating effect — the student has not yet differentiated the two distinct effects of electric current.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with reading the scenario can be asked to re-enact the switch open/close sequence with the physical setup before answering. Students who answer correctly can be extended by asking them to predict what would happen if the wire were replaced with a plastic rod.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe and record the magnetic effect of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe, with reference to their own observations, that a current-carrying conductor produces a magnetic field and that the field disappears when the current is switched off.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: Hans Christian Oersted discovered an important connection between electricity and magnetism in 1820. Which of the following best states what he discovered?

options.label: A
options.text: A coil of wire wrapped around an iron nail becomes a permanent magnet.

options.label: B
options.text: A magnet can produce an electric current in a nearby wire.

options.label: C
options.text: An electric current flowing through a conductor produces a magnetic field around it.

options.label: D
options.text: Two parallel wires carrying current attract or repel each other.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a reversal of the direction of the discovery — the student has confused electromagnetic induction (moving magnet produces current) with Oersted's finding (current produces magnetic field), conflating two distinct phenomena from the chapter.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals recall of a related but different electromagnetic phenomenon — parallel wires and force between them — not covered in this chapter, suggesting the student is drawing on outside knowledge or guessing.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option confuses the electromagnet application (nail wrapped in wire) with Oersted's foundational discovery, which involved a straight wire and compass rather than a coil and nail.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure can be asked to recall the compass-under-wire activity and describe what they saw — this grounds the abstract historical statement in their own experience. Students who answer quickly can be asked to state what technology became possible because of Oersted's discovery.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of electromagnets
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the poles of an electromagnet, demonstrate that reversing the current reverses the poles, and explain how increasing current magnitude or number of turns increases the electromagnet's strength.

competency.competency_text: Investigating properties of natural and artificial magnets; Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Condition | Number of cells | Number of turns | Paper clips held
P | 1 | 20 | 4
Q | 2 | 20 | 9
R | 1 | 40 | 8
S | 2 | 40 | 18
assessment_items.question_text: A student investigates how the strength of an electromagnet changes. Refer to the table provided. Which conclusion is best supported by comparing conditions P and R?

options.label: A
options.text: Both cells and turns must be increased together to produce any increase in strength.

options.label: B
options.text: Increasing the number of cells while keeping turns constant increases the electromagnet's strength.

options.label: C
options.text: Increasing the number of turns while keeping the number of cells constant increases the electromagnet's strength.

options.label: D
options.text: The number of paper clips held is determined only by the total number of turns, regardless of cell count.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals that the student did not identify which variable changed between P and R — they confused the cells comparison (P vs Q) with the turns comparison (P vs R), showing they have not yet learned to read controlled experiments.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals an overgeneralisation: the student ignores the cell-count variable and claims turns are the only factor, contradicting the data pattern visible in comparing P with Q.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals a belief that variables interact multiplicatively and cannot be separated — the student has not applied the concept of controlled variable testing that underpins the investigation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with table reading can be asked to first circle the row pairs that share the same cell count before drawing a conclusion. Students ready for extension can be asked to identify which single condition change between P and S has the largest effect on strength.

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of electromagnets
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the poles of an electromagnet, demonstrate that reversing the current reverses the poles, and explain how increasing current magnitude or number of turns increases the electromagnet's strength.

competency.competency_text: Investigating properties of natural and artificial magnets; Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: A student identifies the North pole of an electromagnet using a compass. She then swaps the battery terminals so that current flows in the opposite direction through the coil. What will she observe when she tests the poles again with the compass?

options.label: A
options.text: The electromagnet gains an additional pole at the centre of the coil.

options.label: B
options.text: The electromagnet loses both its poles because reversing the current cancels the magnetic field.

options.label: C
options.text: The North and South poles of the electromagnet switch to the opposite ends.

options.label: D
options.text: The poles remain the same because the iron core holds the magnetism in a fixed direction.

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option confuses reversing the current with turning off the current — the student has not distinguished direction of current flow from presence of current, suggesting the observation from the pole-reversal activity was not processed causally.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals the alternative conception that the iron core stores magnetism permanently, equivalent to believing the electromagnet behaves like a permanent magnet — a key misconception the pole-reversal activity was designed to address.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option has no basis in the chapter and indicates the student is guessing or drawing on an unrelated conception of magnetic poles.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain can be asked to re-enact the swap using the physical electromagnet setup to observe the result before answering. An extension prompt for confident students: why is this pole-reversibility property essential for the crane lifting electromagnet application?

assessment_items.stage_label: Classify and compare properties of electromagnets
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can identify the poles of an electromagnet, demonstrate that reversing the current reverses the poles, and explain how increasing current magnitude or number of turns increases the electromagnet's strength.

competency.competency_text: Investigating properties of natural and artificial magnets; Earth as a magnet.

assessment_items.question_text: A crane uses a lifting electromagnet to move scrap metal in a factory. The crane operator needs to release the metal at a specific location. Explain why an electromagnet is better suited to this task than a permanent bar magnet, using at least two properties of electromagnets established in this chapter.
expected_elements: The electromagnet's field can be switched off by opening the circuit, allowing the metal to be released on demand — a permanent magnet cannot be switched off.
The strength of the electromagnet can be controlled by adjusting the current or the number of coil turns, allowing it to lift loads of different weights — a permanent magnet has fixed strength.
The poles of the electromagnet can be reversed by reversing the current direction, offering additional control — a permanent magnet cannot do this.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find writing challenging can give their answer as a labelled diagram showing the circuit open and closed states with an explanation of what happens to the metal in each. Students who address only one property can be prompted: 'what else about the electromagnet did you investigate that gives the operator more control?'

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe, record, and explain the heating effect of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why a current-carrying conductor heats up in terms of resistance converting electrical energy to heat, and can classify given scenarios as examples of the heating effect being used beneficially or causing harm.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A nichrome wire is connected in a circuit and current is passed through it. The wire becomes noticeably warm. What is the correct explanation for why the wire heats up?

options.label: A
options.text: The wire heats up because it offers resistance to the flow of current, converting electrical energy to heat energy.

options.label: B
options.text: The wire heats up because nichrome is a magnetic material and the current magnetises it, producing heat.

options.label: C
options.text: The wire heats up because the battery pushes charges so fast that they collide with each other and generate heat.

options.label: D
options.text: The wire heats up because the current itself is hot and transfers its heat to the wire.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals the misconception that heat is a property of current itself rather than a result of the interaction between current and the conductor's resistance — the student has not engaged with the energy conversion mechanism.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option reveals a confusion between the magnetic effect (covered earlier in the chapter) and the heating effect — the student is conflating two separate phenomena and incorrectly attributing heating to magnetism.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals a partially correct intuition (something about collisions) but conflates charge-carrier collisions with the conductor's atomic lattice (resistance) with collisions among charges themselves — an imprecise model that bypasses the resistance concept.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who recall the nichrome wire activity can be asked to describe in their own words what they felt before and after the switch closed, then asked which option matches that experience mechanistically. Extension: ask students to predict which wire would heat more — a longer one or a shorter one of the same material — and justify their prediction.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe, record, and explain the heating effect of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why a current-carrying conductor heats up in terms of resistance converting electrical energy to heat, and can classify given scenarios as examples of the heating effect being used beneficially or causing harm.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Scenario | Device or situation
P | An electric room heater warms the room by glowing red
Q | The long transmission wire from a power station loses energy as it carries current to the city
R | An electric iron uses a coil of resistance wire to press clothes
S | A plastic component inside a circuit board melts when too much current flows through it
assessment_items.question_text: Refer to the table provided. Which pair of scenarios represents the heating effect of electric current being used as the intended, useful output of the device?

options.label: A
options.text: P and Q

options.label: B
options.text: P and R

options.label: C
options.text: Q and S

options.label: D
options.text: R and S

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals that the student correctly identifies P as useful but incorrectly classifies Q as useful — they have not recognised that energy loss in transmission wires is a harmful, unintended consequence rather than a designed output.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals the student has not identified any useful heating application — both Q and S are harmful scenarios — suggesting they may hold the misconception that the heating effect is always undesirable.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option correctly identifies R as a useful application but pairs it with S (a harmful scenario), suggesting the student is uncertain about the distinction between designed heating elements and accidental overheating.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who find the table challenging can be asked to first mark each scenario with a U (useful) or H (harmful) before selecting an option. For extension, ask students to redesign scenario Q to reduce the harmful heating effect.

assessment_items.stage_label: Observe, record, and explain the heating effect of electric current
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can explain why a current-carrying conductor heats up in terms of resistance converting electrical energy to heat, and can classify given scenarios as examples of the heating effect being used beneficially or causing harm.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A student connects two different wires of the same length in a circuit, one at a time: first a thick copper wire and then a thin nichrome wire. She observes that the nichrome wire becomes much hotter than the copper wire when the same current is passed. Using the resistance mechanism explained in this chapter, explain why the nichrome wire heats more, identifying at least two factors that contribute to the difference.
expected_elements: Nichrome is a higher-resistance material than copper, so it converts more electrical energy to heat for the same current.
The nichrome wire is thinner, which increases its resistance further compared to the thicker copper wire.
Greater resistance means more electrical energy is converted to heat energy per unit of current — the resistance mechanism — so the nichrome wire heats significantly more.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write an explanation can be asked to first sort the two wires on a scale of 'more resistance / less resistance' before explaining the heating difference. Students who correctly address both factors can be extended by asking what would happen to the heat produced if the same nichrome wire were cut to half its length.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain how cells and batteries supply the current that drives both effects
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the structure of a Voltaic cell and a dry cell, explain how a chemical reaction between electrodes and electrolyte produces current, and compare the three cell types on key structural and functional properties.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: In the lemon cell activity, a copper wire and an iron nail are pushed into a lemon and connected to an LED. Which component of the lemon acts in the same role as the electrolyte in a Voltaic cell, and what does it do?

options.label: A
options.text: The copper wire acts as the electrolyte by carrying current through the external circuit.

options.label: B
options.text: The iron nail acts as the electrolyte because iron reacts with the lemon to produce electrons directly.

options.label: C
options.text: The LED acts as the electrolyte because it completes the circuit and allows current to flow.

options.label: D
options.text: The lemon juice acts as the electrolyte by enabling a chemical reaction between the two different metal electrodes that produces electricity.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option confuses the external circuit conductor (copper wire) with the electrolyte — the student has not distinguished the role of the medium in which the chemical reaction occurs from the conductors that carry current externally.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option partially identifies the iron nail as a reactive component (correct — it is one electrode) but misidentifies it as the electrolyte rather than as one of the two electrodes, conflating the role of electrode with the role of electrolyte.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option confuses the LED's role (load that uses the current) with the electrolyte's role (medium enabling the internal chemical reaction), suggesting the student has not mapped the Voltaic cell structure onto the lemon cell assembly.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain can be asked to draw their lemon cell and label the part that is inside the lemon versus the parts outside it, then identify which inside component is the liquid medium. Extension: ask what would happen to current production if both electrodes were made of the same metal.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain how cells and batteries supply the current that drives both effects
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the structure of a Voltaic cell and a dry cell, explain how a chemical reaction between electrodes and electrolyte produces current, and compare the three cell types on key structural and functional properties.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A dry cell is described in the chapter as having a moist paste electrolyte instead of a liquid electrolyte. What is the main practical advantage of using a paste electrolyte rather than a liquid one?

options.label: A
options.text: A paste electrolyte allows the cell to be recharged many times without the chemicals being used up.

options.label: B
options.text: A paste electrolyte makes the cell more portable because it will not spill even when the cell is tilted or moved.

options.label: C
options.text: A paste electrolyte prevents the zinc container from acting as the negative terminal of the cell.

options.label: D
options.text: A paste electrolyte produces more electricity than a liquid electrolyte for the same electrode materials.

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals a misconception that the physical state of the electrolyte determines the amount of electricity produced — the student has confused the structural design feature (portability through paste) with energy output.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option conflates the dry cell with rechargeable batteries — the chapter explicitly states that a dry cell is single-use and that rechargeability is a property of a different, more advanced cell type.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option misidentifies the structural role of the zinc container — the chapter clearly states the zinc container is the negative terminal, and the paste electrolyte has no effect on terminal assignment.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure can be asked to recall the comparison table they completed and look at the electrolyte row. Extension: ask students to identify one drawback of using a paste electrolyte compared to a liquid one in a situation where high current output is needed.

assessment_items.stage_label: Explain how cells and batteries supply the current that drives both effects
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can describe the structure of a Voltaic cell and a dry cell, explain how a chemical reaction between electrodes and electrolyte produces current, and compare the three cell types on key structural and functional properties.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A student says: 'A rechargeable battery is completely different from a dry cell — it works on a totally different principle.' Using the structural information about both cell types from this chapter, agree or disagree with this statement and justify your answer in two to three sentences.
expected_elements: Disagree: both the dry cell and the rechargeable battery use the same fundamental principle — two electrodes and an electrolyte where a chemical reaction produces electric current.

The key difference is that in a rechargeable battery the chemical reaction is reversible, so the cell can be restored by supplying electrical energy; in a dry cell the reaction is not reversible and the cell must be discarded when chemicals are used up.
The chapter identifies this difference as one of design (reversibility of the reaction) rather than a difference in the underlying electricity-from-chemistry principle.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find it difficult to formulate a disagreement argument can be asked to first list one similarity and one difference between the two cell types before writing their justification. For extension, ask students to explain why even a rechargeable battery eventually cannot be recharged further.

assessment_items.stage_label: Reason across both effects to explain how cells and electromagnets work as integrated systems
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct and explain an integrated account of how a cell supplies current that produces both magnetic and heating effects, predicting and justifying how changes to cell count, coil turns, or wire material alter each effect.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A circuit contains a single cell, a switch, a coiled wire around an iron nail (electromagnet), and a nichrome wire connected in series. The switch is closed. A student adds a second cell to the circuit. Which of the following correctly predicts what will happen to BOTH effects simultaneously?

options.label: A
options.text: Both effects stay the same because the cell count only affects how long the circuit runs, not how strong the effects are.

options.label: B
options.text: The electromagnet becomes stronger and the nichrome wire gets hotter, because both effects depend on the magnitude of current and adding a cell increases the current.

options.label: C
options.text: The electromagnet becomes stronger but the nichrome wire gets cooler, because the extra cell shares its energy between the two components.

options.label: D
options.text: The electromagnet stays the same strength but the nichrome wire gets hotter, because only the heating effect depends on the number of cells.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals the misconception that energy is divided among components so that one gains at the expense of another — the student has not applied the understanding that increasing current through the whole series circuit increases both effects simultaneously.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals a partial understanding: the student correctly connects cells to heating but has not integrated the earlier finding that electromagnet strength also increases with current (more cells = more current = stronger field).
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals the misconception that the number of cells affects only the duration of operation, not the intensity of current — the student has not connected cell count to current magnitude as established across both strands of the chapter.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are unsure can be asked to answer two separate sub-questions first: 'what does adding a cell do to the current?' and 'what does more current do to the electromagnet?', then 'what does more current do to the heating wire?' before combining. Extension: ask what would happen to only the heating effect if the coil turns were doubled while keeping cells constant.

assessment_items.stage_label: Reason across both effects to explain how cells and electromagnets work as integrated systems
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct and explain an integrated account of how a cell supplies current that produces both magnetic and heating effects, predicting and justifying how changes to cell count, coil turns, or wire material alter each effect.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: An engineer wants to increase the strength of an electromagnet in a device without increasing the temperature of the nichrome heating wire already in the same series circuit. Which change would best achieve this goal?

options.label: A
options.text: Add more cells to the circuit.

options.label: B
options.text: Increase the number of turns on the electromagnet coil while keeping the number of cells the same.

options.label: C
options.text: Replace the iron nail core with a copper rod.

options.label: D
options.text: Use a thinner nichrome wire to increase the heating effect and redirect that energy to the magnet.

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option reveals that the student correctly links cells to electromagnet strength but has not reasoned that adding cells increases current throughout the series circuit, which would also increase the heating of the nichrome wire — the constraint is violated.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option reveals a misconception that any metal core increases field strength; the chapter establishes that only iron (ferromagnetic material) provides the core enhancement — copper would not increase strength.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option reveals a fundamental confusion: the student incorrectly believes that increasing the heating of one component redirects energy to strengthen the magnet — conflating two separate and simultaneous effects of the same current rather than recognising them as independent outcomes.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students can be guided to draw the circuit and label which components are affected by current magnitude versus which are affected only by coil design before choosing. Extension: ask students to explain why the constraint 'without increasing the nichrome wire temperature' rules out adding more cells.

assessment_items.stage_label: Reason across both effects to explain how cells and electromagnets work as integrated systems
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct and explain an integrated account of how a cell supplies current that produces both magnetic and heating effects, predicting and justifying how changes to cell count, coil turns, or wire material alter each effect.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.question_text: A student claims: 'The chapter about electricity is really two separate topics — one about magnets and one about heating. They have nothing to do with each other.' Write a response to this claim. In your response, identify what the two effects have in common at the level of their source and their mechanism, use at least one specific piece of evidence from your activities in this chapter, and explain why a cell or battery is essential to both effects.
look_for: The student explicitly identifies electric current — produced by a cell — as the shared source of both effects, not just mentions both effects separately.
The student references at least one specific activity outcome as evidence (e.g., compass deflection in Activity 4.1, nichrome wire heating in Activity 4.5, or the lemon cell powering an LED).
The student explains why the cell is essential: the chemical reaction in the cell produces current, and without current neither the magnetic field nor the heating occurs.
The student goes beyond listing the two effects to articulate a causal chain: cell → current → effect (magnetic or heating), showing integration rather than juxtaposition.

Stronger responses note that the magnitude of current from the cell controls the strength of both effects, so changing the cell count changes both simultaneously — the effects are linked through their shared dependence on current magnitude.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to write a connected response can be asked to answer three sub-questions in order before drafting: (1) what produces the current? (2) what does current do to a wire wrapped around an iron nail? (3) what does current do to a nichrome wire? — then asked to connect all three into a paragraph. Students who produce a strong response can be asked to extend it by predicting a scenario in which both effects would fail simultaneously and explaining why.

assessment_items.stage_label: Reason across both effects to explain how cells and electromagnets work as integrated systems
assessment_items.implied_lo_assessed: Students can construct and explain an integrated account of how a cell supplies current that produces both magnetic and heating effects, predicting and justifying how changes to cell count, coil turns, or wire material alter each effect.

competency.competency_text: Describing how electricity works and demonstrating its heating and magnetic effects.

assessment_items.visual_stimulus:
Circuit | Cell count | Coil turns | Wire material | Compass clips held (electromagnet) | Wire temperature (heating)
A | 1 | 20 | Nichrome | 4 | Warm
B | 2 | 20 | Nichrome | ? | ?
C | 1 | 40 | Nichrome | ? | ?
D | 1 | 20 | Copper | ? | ?
E | 2 | 40 | Nichrome | ? | ?
assessment_items.task: Refer to the table provided. Circuit A has been tested and its results are shown. Circuits B, C, D, and E have not yet been tested. For each untested circuit: (1) predict the number of clips held and the wire temperature (warmer, same, or cooler than A), and (2) write a one-sentence justification for each prediction, using what you know about how current, coil turns, and wire material affect each effect.
assessment_items.scaffold: Use these ideas to guide your predictions: — Adding cells increases current, which increases both electromagnet strength and heat produced. — Adding coil turns increases electromagnet strength but does not change the current through the circuit, so it does not change the wire temperature. — Replacing nichrome with copper reduces resistance, so the wire heats less; but the current and therefore the electromagnet strength stay the same. — Circuit E combines two changes: reason through each change separately first.
format_of_output: Completed prediction table with entries for circuits B, C, D, and E
One justification sentence per circuit per effect column

OPEN_TASK.format_type: Data interpretation task (provided table or graph)
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Final Stage implied LO requires students to predict and justify how changes to cell count, coil turns, and wire material alter both effects simultaneously — a data table with one complete reference row and four incomplete rows is the most natural vehicle for this multi-variable integrated reasoning without requiring any physical equipment.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: A complete response demonstrates that the student can reason from known values across two independent causal pathways simultaneously: the current-dependent pathway (affecting both effects) and the coil-turns or material pathway (affecting only one effect), integrating across the chapter's two central strands.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold separates the four governing rules so students can apply them sequentially to each circuit. Circuit E is deliberately placed last because it requires reasoning about two simultaneous changes — it functions as a discriminating item that separates students who can integrate from those who can reason only about isolated changes.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong responses correctly identify that changing only coil turns (Circuit C) affects electromagnet strength but not wire temperature, and that changing only wire material (Circuit D) affects wire temperature but not clip count — showing that the student has internalised the independence of the two causal pathways. Weak responses apply the same directional change to both columns for every circuit, suggesting the student believes that any change to the circuit affects both effects equally.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find the full table overwhelming can be asked to complete only circuits B and D first — one that changes current and one that changes material — before attempting the others. Students who complete all five circuits correctly can be asked to design a Circuit F that achieves the maximum possible electromagnet strength with the minimum possible wire temperature, and justify their design.
